what_it_does: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is an AI model architecture where instead of one large neural network doing all the work, the model is divided into many specialist sub-networks ('experts'), and for each input only a small subset of experts is activated — saving compute. However, on systems built from multiple small chiplets (small interconnected chips glued together, increasingly common as transistor scaling slows), each token (word piece) may need to be routed to an expert on a different chiplet, causing massive data-shuffling traffic between chiplets. Hydra tackles this with two ideas: on the software side, it places popular experts on chiplets so that routing decisions minimize how much data crosses chiplet boundaries; on the hardware side, it uses a content-addressable memory (a special memory that can look up entries by value rather than address, like finding a word by its meaning rather than its page number) to avoid an expensive step where outputs need to be unscrambled after parallel processing, and a smarter gate-score calculator that skips unnecessary math for experts with negligible probability of being chosen.
